name: Red blood cell
blurb: A human red blood cell: a disc thinner in the middle than at the rim, with no nucleus, packed with haemoglobin.
note: Model: a human red blood cell, cut through its middle. Measured in human blood: its outline (the Evans–Fung shape, 7.8 µm across), its volume and the number and size of its haemoglobin molecules. Illustrative: the colours, the thickness drawn for the membrane and the spectrin net under it (in life a few nanometres), and the tilt.

diameter.note: 2 x R0 = 2 x 3.91 µm; the range is that of 500 healthy cells measured by holographic microscopy (mean 7.43 µm)

max_thickness.calc: the Evans-Fung profile with the coefficients above, at 2.7 µm from the axis

volume.calc: the volume of the profile turned about its axis

surface_area.calc: the area of the profile turned about its axis

nucleus.note: A mature human red blood cell has no nucleus.

special.note: About 300 million haemoglobin molecules per cell (openstax_rbc). Their size: the extent of the atoms of the 4HHB structure along its three main axes (calculated from data/proteins/4hhb.json). Drawn only where the view is under 0.3 µm across, in a thin layer behind the cut face, at the spacing that number gives (about 6.6 nm between centres).
Under the membrane: a mostly six-sided net of short actin filaments joined by spectrin (liu1987). Drawn as one band along the cut edge; the mesh itself is not drawn.

cut: A cut through the axis of the disc: the section is a dumbbell, thick at the rim and thin in the middle, filled with haemoglobin; the membrane and the spectrin net run round its edge.

colours.convention: Haemoglobin red (a red blood cell is red because of it); the membrane pale; the spectrin net light orange so it shows against the haemoglobin. Only the red of the haemoglobin is the real colour; the rest is a code.

spectrin.name: Spectrin net
spectrin.about: Under the membrane a net of spectrin, a long flexible protein, holds the cell's shape: mostly six-sided meshes whose corners are short actin filaments. It lets the cell bend through capillaries narrower than itself and spring back.

about: The outline is the Evans–Fung formula for a healthy human red blood cell (diameter 7.82 µm). Turned about its axis it gives a volume of {drawn.cellVolume} µm³; 500 healthy cells measured by holographic microscopy averaged 86 ± 14 µm³ (femtolitres).

There is no nucleus and there are no mitochondria: the cell is a bag of haemoglobin, about 300 million molecules of it. Come close to the cut face (under 0.3 µm across) and the molecules are drawn at their true size and spacing.
The membrane and the spectrin net are drawn as bands thick enough to see; in life each is only a few nanometres thick.

evansfung.cite: Totero Gongora JS, Fratalocchi A (2016) Optical force on diseased blood cells: towards the optical sorting of biological matter, arXiv:1605.04509 (Evans-Fung coefficients of a healthy, isotonic red blood cell, from Evans E, Fung YC 1972, Microvasc Res 4:335)
evansfung.used_for: R0 = 3.91 µm, C0 = 0.81 µm, C2 = 7.38 µm, C4 = -4.39 µm (the 1972 paper itself was not opened)

bhabhor.cite: Bhabhor GD, Patel C, Chhillar N, Anand A, Lad KN (2023) Geometrical characterization of healthy red blood cells using digital holographic microscopy and parametric shape models, arXiv:2301.12879
bhabhor.used_for: 500 healthy cells: diameter 6.0-9.0 µm (mean 7.43), maximum thickness 3.23 ± 0.48 µm, volume 86.1 ± 14.0 fL, surface 121.2 ± 10.8 µm²

openstax_rbc.used_for: biconcave disc about 7-8 µm across; no nucleus, mitochondria or ER; about 300 million haemoglobin molecules per cell; lives up to 120 days

liu1987.cite: Liu SC, Derick LH, Palek J (1987) Visualization of the hexagonal lattice in the erythrocyte membrane skeleton, J Cell Biol 104:527
liu1987.used_for: a mainly hexagonal lattice of junctional actin complexes cross-linked by spectrin (abstract)

pdb_4hhb.cite: Fermi G, Perutz MF, Shaanan B, Fourme R (1984) The crystal structure of human deoxyhaemoglobin at 1.74 Å resolution, PDB 4HHB (data/proteins/4hhb.json)
pdb_4hhb.used_for: the size of one haemoglobin molecule: 5.4 x 5.7 x 6.6 nm, the extent of its atom centres along its principal axes (calculated)
